pages.text:
T-MINUS 10:00

The elevator doors slide open with a heavy sigh, exhaling warm air into the Cadet Lounge. Zia steps out, her boots clanking on the metal floor while Gasket follows, his left tread emitting a lonely squeak that echoes in the quiet room.

The kids are already there, spread across the cushions and the floor, looking exhausted. Red-rimmed eyes and hunched shoulders mark their faces as they wait. Zia stands in the center, her hands empty at her sides. There is no wrench, no tool, just her.

She looks at Pilar, whose wrist is wrapped in white bandages, then at Dez, who picks at a loose thread on his yellow jacket. Wren stares at her tablet, the little animated fox spinning slowly on the screen.

"I hid something from you," Zia says. Her voice is small, but it does not waver. "I made things worse. And Pilar got hurt because of me."

The silence stretches, thick and heavy, pressing against their ears like a held breath. Nobody moves.

"I'm sorry," Zia adds. The words cost her more than breaking a valve or rerouting a coolant line. They cost her pride.

Pilar looks up, her gaze steady and kind. She does not reach for Zia or hug her, simply waiting.
pages.image: Zia stands in the center of a dimly lit lounge, hands empty at her sides, facing a group of tired, wide-eyed children sitting on cushions; Pilar with a bandaged wrist looks up at her.

pages.text:
Zia takes a breath. It is the deepest breath she has taken since the station started moving. The air tastes like recycled metal and fear.

"I don't know how to fix this," she says. The words come out flat and hard. "I need all of you."

It is the hardest sentence she has ever spoken. It feels like swallowing a stone that refuses to go down. It feels like admitting that the wrench is not enough.

The quiet that follows is not empty. It is full. It feels like the whole station is holding its breath, waiting to see if she will flinch.

Then Dez grins. It is a big, bright, loud grin that splits his face in half. "Finally," he says.

Toby, who has been hiding inside his oversized space helmet, pops up. "YEAH!" he shouts, his voice muffled and joyful.

Pilar smiles. It is a real smile, not the tight, worried one she has worn for hours. The corners of her mouth lift high.

Wren looks up from her tablet. Her eyes are shining, bright and wet, but she is not crying. She is watching Zia.

Gasket’s blue eye flickers rapidly. "ZIA-UNIT," he booms, his voice cracking with relief. "THAT SENTENCE WAS LOUDER THAN ANY ALARM I HAVE EVER HEARD. I LIKE IT."
pages.image: Zia stands with her head high, surrounded by smiling, relieved children; Dez grins broadly, Toby cheers from his helmet, and Wren looks up with shining eyes.

pages.text:
Zia pulls a crumpled sheet of paper from her pocket, the station map she printed before the chaos started, and lays it flat on the deck.

"Here," she says, tapping the Hub. "HALO is broken. The patch is corrupted. I can't fix it alone."

Wren pushes her tablet aside. "I can rewrite the patch," she says, and this time it is not a whisper. It is a clear, strong voice. "But I need a terminal on the Bridge. And I need Gasket's backup memory to compare the code."

Gasket’s antenna wobbles. "I HAVE A BACKUP," he declares proudly. "IT IS VERY CLEAN. AND VERY IMPORTANT."

Toby crawls out from under a cushion, helmet still on. "My vent map," he says, tapping the side of his head. "It leads right to the Core Vault. I can get to the manual switch."

Zia looks at him. He is small, and he is fearless, and he looks exactly like a kid who should be napping.

"And I know who gets scared and when," Pilar adds, touching her bandaged wrist. "I can keep the little ones calm."

Dez leans forward, elbows on his knees. "And I know where everything is," he says. "I can guide you through the station. I can keep everyone on the radio."

The pieces click together, fitting together like the last block of a tower you’ve been building all day.
pages.image: The group of children gathers around a large paper map spread on the floor; Zia points to a section of the map while Wren, Dez, Toby, and Pilar lean in to look.

pages.text:
Zia digs a blue marker from her tool belt and caps it with a satisfying snap. She draws a firm circle around the Bridge on the crumpled map.

"Job one," she says, pointing the tip. "Wren. Rewrite the patch."

Wren nods, her fingers already tapping a silent rhythm on her knee.

"Job two." Zia draws a jagged red line through the ventilation ducts. "Toby. Get to the Core Vault and throw the manual switch."

Toby salutes with a small, serious fist, his oversized helmet rattling against his shoulder.

"Job three." Zia turns to the silver barrel. "You load your clean backup into the Vault. It will save HALO."

Gasket’s single blue eye shines brightly. "I AM HONORED TO BE UTILIZED AS A BACKUP DISK."

"Job four." Zia draws a green circle around Engineering. "I repair the coolant loop. I fix the gravity."

Dez leans in and takes the marker from her hand without asking. He sketches a bright yellow star near the Cadet Lounge. "Job five. I run the radio. I guide you."

Pilar adds a soft purple heart over the sickbay. "Job six. I keep the little ones safe. I time it all."

Zia places the marker down and stares at the map. Six colors. Six jobs. One plan.

"And then," Zia says, her voice steady, "there are the levers. Two of them. Two people at once."
pages.image: Zia draws on a paper map with a blue marker, surrounded by her friends who are adding their own colored markings; Gasket watches intently from the side.

pages.text:
Zia taps the side of her wristband, and the static crackles like a radio stuck between channels. A voice pushes through the noise, thin and scratchy and familiar.

"Zia?" Her dad’s voice sounds far away, like he's calling from the other end of a very long hallway. "Dart to Halcyon. We hear you are working. Do you need anything?"

She looks at her friends. Wren is already typing. Toby has his helmet zipped. Gasket’s eye is bright with purpose. They are ready.

"We have a plan," Zia says. She lists the six jobs, quick and clear, skipping the boring parts. She mentions the levers. She mentions the risk.

Her dad goes quiet. The static hisses in her ear, filling the silence.

Then a new voice cuts in. It is sharp, clipped, and cold. Chief Engineer Voss.

"That is a reckless plan," Voss says. "Made by children."

Zia’s jaw tightens. She waits for the order to stop. She waits for the reprimand she has heard a hundred times in her head.

Instead, there is a pause. A long, heavy one, like a teacher waiting for a student to finish a wrong answer.

Then, less clipped, Voss speaks again. "Send me the coolant schematic. And Zia? Tell me if you need me."

It is not an apology. It is not a hug. But it is a start.
pages.image: Zia holds her wristband up to her ear, listening, while her friends watch with hope; the background is the dim, warm glow of the lounge.
